RisingWave has no transaction around DML and an INSERT onto an existing key is an upsert, so this was invisible until a test asserted on the two retentions. A citation by evidence_id now resolves to one row per endpoint that retrieved it: the same claim, retrieved twice, which is what happened.

task 35: STATUS IS DERIVED AT READ TIME, AND THE PRECEDENT WAS ALREADY IN THE TREE. `helena.enrichment.feed_status` computes ok/stale/missing from the ledger rather than storing them, with the argument in its docstring: 'a stored stale would be wrong the moment time passed.' It is sharper for a cache, because a cached claim crosses from ok to stale with NO WRITER INVOLVED. So the cache table has retrieved_at and expires_at and no status column, and it lines up with evidence_id already excluding the status — a claim that goes stale is the same claim.

task 35: THE SAFETY RULE FOR CACHE-KEY NORMALIZATION IS AN ASYMMETRY, NOT A LIST. A fold that is too timid costs one live query and one re-disclosure of an already-disclosed indicator. A fold that is too eager serves ONE INDICATOR'S EVIDENCE FOR A DIFFERENT INDICATOR — a wrong answer with a citation on it. So: fold only what the identifier's own specification makes equivalent, and when in doubt leave the value exactly as it is. That rule is what decides the hard cases (a URL fragment stays, an IDN's two forms stay two keys, a value that will not parse is returned untouched) without needing a judgement call per case.

task 35: THE DISCLOSURE MEASUREMENT IS THE ADAPTER, NOT A COUNTER. `helena.tools` imports no HTTP machinery at all (asserted off the module's own AST, task 34's test), so the injected adapter is the ONLY thing in the layer that can reach a provider. An adapter that was not called is therefore an indicator that was not sent, which turns 'a cache hit discloses nothing' into a property a test can hold rather than a sentence in a docstring.

task 35: STORING THE RESPONSE BEFORE EVALUATING IT IS LOAD-BEARING, AND THE MALFORMED CASE IS WHAT PROVES IT. A response that will not map into the declared subset ends up on disk under its digest with NO claims beside it. Two things fall out for free: the operator can investigate the failure against what actually arrived, and the next lookup is still a miss — because the cache read requires at least one claim, a stored-but-unmappable response can never be served as an answer.

task 35: MAKING A DEPENDENCY REQUIRED IN A 40-TEST MODULE COSTS ONE AUTOUSE FIXTURE, NOT 40 SIGNATURES. `ProviderTool` takes a required `cache`, because 'every provider tool is cache-first' and an optional one is a tool that is not. tests/test_tools.py gained `pytestmark = pytest.mark.integration`, an autouse fixture that pushes `migrated_engine` onto a module-level handle, and one line in the `tool()` builder. `migrated_engine` empties data tables rather than re-migrating, so 47 unit tests becoming integration tests cost about 20 s, not minutes.

task 35: RISINGWAVE 3.0.3 BYTEA ROUND-TRIPS EXACTLY, INCLUDING NUL AND INVALID UTF-8, and psycopg returns `memoryview` — `bytes(row[0])` is needed before comparing. Measured before the migration was written, which is why the retained response is BYTEA and not TEXT: an encoding guess at the store boundary would be a re-encoding nobody recorded, on the one payload that exists to be compared against what the provider actually sent.

task 36: SPENT IS NOT TRUNCATED, and the difference decides whether a good verdict survives. A dimension whose remainder reached zero is not the same as a run that asked for more and was refused: the first is a run that finished, the second is the one `concept/07` degrades to `unknown`. `RunBudget.exhausted` records refusals only, and `record_tokens` (which reports spending that already happened) marks nothing. Collapsing the two turns 'used its budget efficiently' into 'unassessable'.

task 36: THE ORDER OF THE CHARGES IN THE DISPATCH IS THE DESIGN. A step and the clock before anything else, so an unbounded loop cannot be bought with malformed calls and a finished run does not do work nobody can use; the live query AFTER the cache read, so a hit costs no quota and a run out of quota can still read what it already fetched. That last one is a measured consequence and a test, not an intention.

task 36: ONE LEDGER PER RUN, PASSED IN, NEVER BUILT INSIDE. `assess` used to compute its own deadline from `request.budgets`, which is correct for a single exchange and wrong for a loop: every turn would get the full wall clock again. The fix is a required argument, and the check that makes it safe is `assess` refusing a ledger whose limits are not the request's.

task 36: `model_copy` SKIPS `model_post_init`, so it cannot be used to rewrite a contract object that has rules. `degraded` re-validates through `model_validate_json(json.dumps(...))` — the shape `assess` already uses, because the contracts are `strict=True` and python mode refuses the list a dump produces where a tuple is declared. Written the short way, the degrade could have produced exactly the `normal`-with-a-budget_exhausted-gap outcome `concept/07` forbids, and the contract would never have seen it.

task 36: A DERIVED NUMBER NEEDS ITS INPUTS KEPT. `BudgetPolicy` carries `rate_limits` and `retrieval_seconds` beside the four dimensions so the test recomputes the live-query budget from them rather than comparing it with a number written down twice — which is the same rule as the duplicated-version-constant one, applied to arithmetic.

task 36: TWO LOADERS OVER ONE CONFIG FILE NEED ONE KEY LIST. `policy.thresholds()` refuses a top-level key nothing reads, so adding `[budgets]` to `config/policy.toml` would have made it refuse to start. `helena.policy` now names both `THRESHOLD_KEYS` and `BUDGET_KEYS` (it owns the path), `helena.budgets` imports them, and a test asserts the committed file loads under both.

task 37: THE SEND POLICY'S FIELD LIST IS ONLY WORTH ANYTHING IF THE VOCABULARY IS THE REQUEST'S OWN FIELD SET. `SENDABLE_FIELDS` is asserted equal to `tools.ToolCall.model_fields`, so 'a policy-forbidden field cannot reach a request body' is a property of the code rather than a rule an adapter has to remember: the adapter is handed the `ToolCall` and nothing else, so what the policy withholds is a request that cannot be assembled, and the tenant and the sensor are in no vocabulary at all. A field added to the call later fails that test until it is declared here and permitted in the file.

task 37: PERMISSION AND CAPABILITY ARE TWO REFUSALS AND COLLAPSING THEM WOULD LOSE THE ACTIONABLE ONE. `entity_type_not_covered` is the source's capability ('a JA3 list has nothing to say about a domain') and is fixed by asking a different source; `send_policy_forbids` is this deployment's permission and is fixed by editing `config/policy.toml`. Same shape as the four ways a call produces no claim, and the loader enforces the containment: a permission wider than the capability is refused at load, because a line permitting something the source cannot answer about is one nothing reads.

task 37: A DECLARATION THAT OFFERS WHAT THE DISPATCH WILL REFUSE IS A PROMISE THE LAYER DOES NOT KEEP. `ProviderTool.declaration()` now offers the INTERSECTION of the descriptor's entity types and the policy's, because offering a type every call would be refused for spends a step and a turn of the loop on a refusal the layer could have declined to invite. The model is not told why the set is what it is: a tool description is not where a deployment explains its policy.

task 37: RECORD A DISCLOSURE BEFORE THE SEND, NEVER AFTER. A request that reached the provider (or the model endpoint) and then timed out disclosed the indicator anyway, so recording on success under-records exactly the case an operator most needs to see. The cost is a row for a call that failed before it left the process, which over-records in the direction an audit can live with. Both channels do it in that order and both have a test.

task 37: A CONFIG KEY IN TOML BELONGS TO THE LAST TABLE THAT WAS OPENED. `send_policy_version` appended at the foot of `config/policy.toml` silently became `rate_limits.send_policy_version` and broke two loaders at once; it lives at the top with the other version keys, with a comment saying why. Cheap to hit and easy to miss, because the file still parses.

task 37: THREE LOADERS OVER ONE POLICY FILE NEED THEIR KEY SETS IN ONE PLACE. `helena.policy` owns the path and now names all three sets (`THRESHOLD_KEYS`, `BUDGET_KEYS`, `DISCLOSURE_KEYS`); each loader refuses a key NOTHING reads and none refuses a key another requires, and a test loads the shipped file through all three. Adding a fourth table means adding a set there, not a subtraction in three places.

task 37: `disclosed_to` IS A HOST AND THE LOADER REFUSES A URL. `concept/07` requires a credential travelling in a URL to be redacted before anything is logged or stored, and the strongest version of that rule is that the policy file holds no URL to begin with — the tool layer holds none either. `key@host`, a scheme and a path are all refused at load.

task 37: MEASURING A HOST IS NOT THE SAME AS CONFIRMING A QUERY SURFACE, AND SAYING SO KEEPS TASK 38 HONEST. One unauthenticated POST to `threatfox-api.abuse.ch/api/v1/` returned 401 on 2026-09-09 — that settles WHERE an analyst query would go, which a disclosure record must name, and settles nothing about the request shape, which is what `concept/05` records this project getting wrong repeatedly.

task 37: THE DISCLOSURE LEDGER IS THE CALLER'S BECAUSE THE CONTRACT HAS NOWHERE FOR IT. The budget ledger can be built inside `helena.triage.run` because `AgentResult.cost` carries its product out; a disclosure row has no contract field, so a ledger built inside `run` would be a record that dies at the return statement. The asymmetry is the contract's rather than a preference, and it is where the orchestration increment has to own the object.

task 38: THE THREATFOX HUNTING API, MEASURED 2026-09-10 AND WORTH NOT RE-DISCOVERING: `POST https://threatfox-api.abuse.ch/api/v1/`, JSON body, operation in the `query` key, credential in the `Auth-Key` HEADER. Ten documented operations; `search_ioc` is the per-indicator lookup. HTTP 200 answers EVERY application error — the status carries nothing and `query_status` does — and `data` is a LIST on `ok` and a STRING on `no_result`. Wrong key: HTTP 403 `{"query_status": "unknown_auth_key"}`. No key: HTTP 401 `{"error": "Unauthorized"}`, no `query_status` at all. No rate-limit header on any response.

task 38: `exact_match: true` CAN NEVER MATCH AN ADDRESS. `{"query": "types"}` returns the closed ioc_type vocabulary and there is no bare `ip` in it — only `ip:port`. So an address lookup must use the wildcard, and the wildcard is NOT a substring search and it CROSSES ENTITY TYPES: `72.255.59.61` returned a `url` record containing that address, `workers.dev` returned 1 386 records, and a strict prefix of a listed `ip:port` returned nothing. A wildcard result is a set of CANDIDATES and every one must be checked against the asked indicator and entity type, or a URL listing gets reported as an address claim.

task 38: THE HUNTING API AND THE BULK EXPORT SPELL THE SAME RECORDS DIFFERENTLY, IN FIVE WAYS: `ioc` vs `ioc_value`; `first_seen`/`last_seen` (with a ' UTC' suffix `datetime.fromisoformat` will not read) vs `first_seen_utc`/`last_seen_utc`; `tags` is an ARRAY on the API and a comma-separated STRING on the export; the indicator id is a field on the API and the OBJECT KEY on the export; `anonymous` is export-only, and `sightings`/`threat_type_desc`/`ioc_type_desc`/`malware_malpedia`/`malware_samples` are API-only. Anything written from one surface against the other is wrong in five places.

task 38: THE RETRIEVAL CONFOUND IS MEASURED, NOT ARGUED. Three indicators present in the loaded snapshot were asked of the live API: for all three, EVERY field the two surfaces share was identical — same record id, threat type, malware, confidence, first-seen, compromised flag, reporter. A ThreatFox analyst claim corroborating a ThreatFox enrichment claim is ONE SOURCE AGREEING WITH ITSELF. `source_diversity` counts by `source_id` and both tiers carry `threatfox`, so the arithmetic is right and must stay right. The one field the live surface adds is `sightings`; expiry cuts the other way, since an IOC older than six months is on neither surface while a stale snapshot still holds it.

task 38: THE EXACT MATCH IS CASE-INSENSITIVE BUT REJECTS A TRAILING ROOT DOT. `fuwabo.workers.dev.` is `no_result`. That spelling comes out of DNS legitimately, so an adapter that sends the caller's spelling verbatim caches a `no_match` that is simply wrong — one indicator's absence recorded as another's. Send the value `helena.tools.normalize_indicator` produces.

task 38: THE BULK EXPORT'S AUTH STORY NOW HAS TWO TRUE HALVES ON TWO ENDPOINTS, AND SOMEBODY WILL 'RE-CORRECT' THE 2026-09-03 CORRECTION IF THIS IS NOT WRITTEN DOWN. `GET threatfox.abuse.ch/export/json/recent/` — the one `helena.enrichment.fetch_threatfox` uses — is STILL 200 with no credential, re-measured 2026-09-10, 3 774 281 bytes. But the export index now documents a NEWER surface, `threatfox-api.abuse.ch/v2/files/exports/<AUTH-KEY>/full.csv.zip`, which puts the key IN THE URL PATH. Nothing here uses it. The 2026-09-03 correction was about the endpoint the loader fetches and is still right about it.

task 38: AN `urllib.error.HTTPError` IS ALSO AN OPEN RESPONSE, and it stays open for as long as the exception it is chained to. Under `filterwarnings = ["error"]` that surfaces as a `PytestUnraisableExceptionWarning` about an unclosed socket, at an unrelated test, some time after the one that leaked it. `refused.close()` before raising is the fix; `helena.agents` has the same shape and has not hit it only because its exceptions are not held across tests.

task 39: A `response_format` json_schema AND a `tools` list CANNOT BE SENT TOGETHER on the configured endpoint, measured 2026-09-10: with both, `finish_reason` is `stop` and the model emits the final JSON and calls no tool. The schema compiles to a grammar the model cannot leave. A single-phase tool loop built that way is the worst kind of green suite — it 'works', it never retrieves, and its verdicts look like verdicts. `ModelClient.complete` now takes exactly one of the two and refuses both.

task 39: THE ENDPOINT RETURNS `content: null` ON A TURN THAT IS ONLY A TOOL CALL, and `tool_calls` entries under `choices[0].message.tool_calls` with `function.name` and `function.arguments` as a JSON STRING. `Completion.text` coerces null to '' and keeps `tool_calls` separate: an answer with tool calls is a turn of a loop and one without them is a turn that stopped, and collapsing the two would make 'the model chose to stop' and 'the model said nothing' one fact.

task 39: `max_tokens` IS WHAT THE LEDGER HAS LEFT, AND A REASONING MODEL SPENDS IT BEFORE IT WRITES A CHARACTER. Measured: the same live run at 20 000 tokens produced an EMPTY completion on its last attempt — which surfaces as `schema_invalid` 'the answer is not JSON' — and at 60 000 produced a verdict with no retries. A token budget that looks generous for one call is a truncated answer by the third turn of a loop.

task 39: THE ANALYST'S CLASSIFICATION SET IS THE PATHS, NOT THE ROOTS, and that is the one place its `classifications()` deliberately differs from triage's. `concept/04` gives it a verdict 'with a classification path'; the offered set is every context path whose root is in `emitter_roots[analyst]` and that `for_emission` accepts, so a version-declared-unused path (`suspicious.anomalous_volume` under v1) is never offered rather than offered and then refused.

task 39: THE RETRIEVAL TRACE MUST NOT BE OFFERED TO THE MODEL, and the reason is sharper than 'the code knows it'. `check_exchange` resolves an analyst's citations against the rendering's evidence ids OR ITS OWN RETRIEVAL TRACE — so a model that could write the trace could authorise its own citations. It is excluded from the prompt's field set and `run` refuses a prompt version that offers it.

task 39: A CONTEXT PROJECTION ENTITY CARRIES THE VALUE AS OBSERVED AND A RETRIEVED CLAIM CARRIES IT NORMALIZED (`sql/migrations/0007` takes a DNS `query_name` verbatim; `helena.tools` records a claim against `normalize_indicator`'s fold). So `helena.policy.supports_for` takes analyst-tier claims as (entity, evidence) PAIRS and does not join on the value — joining would silently drop exactly the claims whose spelling the fold changed, and dropping a support is the one thing that function refuses to do quietly.

task 39: NOTHING IN SQL JOINS AN ANALYST-TIER CLAIM TO THE OBSERVED PORTS, because `helena_reference_evidence_analyst` is deliberately not unioned into the enriched context. So `port_matched` needed a Python copy — and the test asserts the two equal BY EXECUTION: `sql/migrations/0015`'s `CASE` is read out of the file, its two column references replaced by parameters, and run against the engine over the same inputs.

task 39: THE LOOP'S TERMINATION IS ARITHMETIC AND NOT A CONSTANT. A turn that produces no tool call ends it; a turn whose calls charged no step ends it too. So every turn that continues has strictly increased `budget.steps_spent`, which `Budgets.steps` bounds — there is no separate turn limit to keep consistent with the step budget, and no way for a model to buy another turn by asking for something that costs nothing.

task 39: EXACTLY ONE STEP PER REQUESTED TOOL CALL, WHOEVER REFUSES IT. `ProviderTool.lookup` charges its own before it validates anything, so the runner charges only for the calls it refuses itself — and it charges BEFORE announcing the refusal, so a run with no step left answers `budget_exhausted` whether the tool it named existed or not. The two layers' answers then agree about which fact ran out first.

task 40: The analyst lookup cache is keyed by tenant AND sensor (`helena.tools.EvidenceCache`), so two runs of the same question inside one test are one run: the second is a cache hit and the provider adapter is never called. A differential test that needs two live provider answers must vary the scope — `request(sensor=...)` plus `a_projection(sensor=...)` is the smallest difference and the prompt cannot see it, because a rendering carries what the host did and never who watched it.

task 40: `helena.broker.Message` and `helena.agents.Message` share a name and nothing else. An AST lint that matches on the call name alone walks into `broker.py` looking for a `content=` that a Kafka record does not have. Resolve the import (`from helena.agents import Message`) or the class definition, not the name.

task 40: Byte-equivalence of a refactor against the previous commit is cheap and worth doing when a frozen file is touched: `git archive HEAD src tests | tar -x -C /tmp/<dir>`, then run the same builder with `/tmp/<dir>/src` and `/tmp/<dir>/tests` at the front of `sys.path`. It takes two minutes and it turns 'the prompt did not change' from a claim into a diff.

task 40: `helena.agents._attempt_messages` sends the model a Pydantic validation error on a retry, and a Pydantic error quotes the `input_value` that failed. That is a route from a model's own words — which may be a copy of what it was shown — back into a prompt. It is framed now, but the general shape is worth remembering: any diagnostic that quotes its input is untrusted text if the input was.

task 40: The full suite is ~9 minutes and only one engine runs per machine, so two concurrent `pytest` processes share one engine and one set of truncations. Do not overlap them; the result of the earlier run cannot be trusted if a second started underneath it.

task 41: REPLAY MODE CANNOT BE ARMED FOR A WHOLE AGENT RUN, AND THE REASON IS THE MODEL. A process-wide socket guard held open across an analyst run would block hosted inference, which is also a network call. So `helena.network.no_network()` is armed by `ProviderTool.lookup` around ONE dispatch and released after it, and the claim it supports is bounded accordingly: nothing new leaves the process while a replay lookup runs. Anything later that wants a whole-run offline assertion has to exempt the model endpoint deliberately, not by accident.

task 41: THE GUARD BLOCKS `connect`, NOT WRITES, AND THAT BOUND IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN LAZY. A replay reads its stored responses out of the streaming engine over a psycopg connection opened before the guard is armed; blocking sends on an already-open socket would make the guard airtight and make replay impossible. `tests/test_replay.py::test_an_already_open_connection_to_the_store_keeps_working_inside_the_guard` executes a real query against the real engine inside the guard, so the bound is pinned by a test rather than left in a docstring. What that means for a later adapter: one holding a pooled connection open across a live phase and a replay phase would slip through. `helena.providers` opens a socket per call, so none does today.

task 41: `helena.tools` MAY NOT IMPORT `socket`, AND THAT IS WHY THE GUARD IS ITS OWN MODULE. `tests/test_tools.py` reads `tools.py`'s AST and fails on `urllib`/`http`/`socket`/`ssl` (task 34), which is what makes 'the agent sees a tool, never an HTTP client and never a key' a property of the code. `helena.providers` is the obvious home and cannot be one — it imports `helena.tools`. `helena/network.py` holds one context manager, one exception, no URL and no client, and is registered in `tests/test_package_layout.py`'s SUPPORT_MODULES with that reasoning. It is NOT named `replay`, because `concept/03` puts 'replays from stored results' in Orchestration and that runner does not exist.

task 41: AN EXPIRED RECORD IS SERVED IN A REPLAY AND CARRIES NO FAILURE STEP. Nothing is ever evicted, so the record is still citable and `concept/02`'s `stale` is exactly what it is. The live path's stale fallback carries a `QueryFailure` beside it because a provider was reached and did not answer; a replay reached nothing, and reporting a timeout nobody experienced would be inventing an outage to explain an age. Found while writing it: `_served` derived its LOG LINE's status from whether a failure was passed — correct for both live callers, wrong the first time a replay served an expired record with no outage. It now derives it from the same expiry the evidence rows are dated against.

task 41: A REPLAY NEEDS THE STORE AND NOT THE CREDENTIAL. The adapter is the only thing the `Secret` is ever handed to, and no branch of a replay reaches it, so a replayed run never reveals the key. That is a property worth keeping when the orchestration replay runner is built: it can run where the provider key is absent.

task 42: THE ORDERING CLAIM 'ESCALATION IS COMPUTED BEFORE TRIAGE' IS TESTABLE BY EXECUTION, AND THE MECHANISM IS THE LOG STREAM. `helena.observability.StructuredLogger` takes a stream, and `helena.agents.ModelClient` takes a logger — so handing the router and both model clients ONE `io.StringIO` makes the order of the lines the order the code ran in. `orchestration.escalation_evaluated` before the first `agents.model.call` is then an observation rather than an assertion about the source. Reusable by anything else in this tree that has an ordering invariant between a deterministic step and a model call.

task 42: THE TWO PROMPT VERSIONS COLLIDE AT `v1`, AND A STORED ROW NEEDS THE EMITTER TO TELL THEM APART. `triage.version('v1')` and `analyst.version('v1')` both report `v1` because a prompt version is per-package. A test asserting that the derived analyst request differs from the triage request in `versions` FAILS today for that reason, and the honest test is a subset assertion plus a note. Anything that reconstructs a prompt from a stored `prompt_version` must key on (emitter, prompt_version), never on the version alone.

task 42: `model_copy(update=...)` DOES NOT RE-VALIDATE IN PYDANTIC v2, so deriving a contract object with it produces the one instance in the system the contract never checked. `analyst_request` rebuilds through `AgentRequest(**fields)` instead, which is what makes `AgentRequest`'s own emitter/trigger pairing check and its triage-budget refusal apply to the derived request too.

task 42: AN ANALYST RUN WITH `provider_tools=()` MAKES EXACTLY ONE MODEL CALL AND NEVER ENTERS THE LOOP (`helena.analyst._retrieve` returns immediately on empty declarations). That is what lets a routing test be a routing test: 24 of the 27 tests here need no engine at all, because a routing assertion needs an analyst that RAN, not one that retrieved.

task 42: THE LOG RECORD'S FIELDS ARE NOT AT THE TOP LEVEL. `helena.observability.StructuredLogger._emit` lifts `event`, `context_id`, `event_id` and `versions` out and puts everything else under `fields`. A test reading a log line has to unwrap once; three tests here go through one helper for it.

task 43: AN ASSESSMENT ROW IS ONE AGENT RUN, NOT ONE PASS THROUGH THE ROUTER. Every column `concept/03` lists — cost, latency, the nine versions, the model that answered, the endpoint, the verdict, the confidence — is a property of one run, and a pass reaches one or two agents with different models, prompts, budgets and costs. A row per pass would carry two of each or lose one. The two rows of one pass share `(tenant, sensor, context_id, context_version)`, which is what D7's 'emitted once, carrying the analyst's verdict and the triage decision that led to it' joins on.

task 43: THE WRITE ORDER IS PART OF THE CONTRACT AND A TEST FOUND IT WRONG. `AssessmentStore._one` deletes and writes the child rows first and the assessment row last, so a visible assessment always has its whole citation set. Everything that can refuse — `check_exchange`, and the two-endpoint check — must therefore run BEFORE the first child insert, or a refusal leaves orphaned children. The first version computed the endpoint host inside the INSERT parameter tuple and did exactly that; it was found by a citation row surviving into the NEXT test, because RisingWave DML is asynchronous and the unflushed inserts outlived the `migrated_engine` fixture's DELETE. Two things to carry: a refusal in a writer has to be ordered against the writes, and an unflushed insert in RisingWave can cross a test boundary.

task 43: THE ENDPOINT HOST IS READ OFF THE RUN'S DISCLOSURE LEDGER, NOT OFF CONFIGURATION. `concept/07` records endpoint and model per assessment so that cross-wiring is detectable — and configuration is exactly what would be wrong in that case, so reading the column from configuration would record the lie. `Disclosure.disclosed_to` on the `model_inference` rows is the record of where bytes actually went. NULL means no prompt ever left the process, which is a different fact from a run that reached an endpoint and failed; two hosts in one ledger is this project's own bug and is loud.

task 43: NULL IS A FIFTH KIND OF ABSENCE AND MONEY IS WHERE IT MATTERS. `model_cost` NULL means 'not priced'; it does not mean free. The whole reason `[model_prices]` ships empty is that a plausible rate in an audit record is worse than an empty column — the same argument `concept/instruction.md` §2 makes about `stale`/`failed`/`missing`/`no_match`, applied to a number.

task 43: THE 'NO FREE-TEXT NOTE' PROPERTY IS THREE TESTS, AND THE THIRD IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. (1) no table or column in the whole schema is named like a note; (2) the free-text columns are a declared six and every other stored string is a closed-vocabulary token, an identifier, a digest or a version, demonstrated over a real run rather than declared; (3) NOTHING THAT BUILDS A PROMPT CAN READ A STORED ASSESSMENT — the three modules `tests/test_untrusted.py` names as the only ones that construct a `helena.agents.Message` are read as ASTs and must not name an assessment table or the store. A bounded narrative that cannot be read back is not a memory-poisoning channel; the same narrative reachable from a prompt builder is one, whatever its length limit says.

task 43: `observation` IS THIS PROJECT'S WORD FOR TRAFFIC, NOT FOR AN AGENT'S PROSE. A note-name regex over the whole schema hits `helena_signal_entity_observations`, which is a measurement table. The loose 'observations' field the agent contract refuses is refused by `extra="forbid"` and by `tests/test_contracts.py`, which is where that rule is checkable by name.

task 43: PERSISTENCE WENT INTO `helena.orchestration` RATHER THAN A NEW MODULE, and that was `tests/test_package_layout.py`'s own instruction: its comment says `orchestration` keeps 'routing, validation, persistence and replay' of `concept/03`'s component row. A new top-level module would have been a deliberate layout edit and an escalation for no gain — the store imports nothing `orchestration` did not already import except `psycopg`.

task 44: AN IDENTIFIER THAT CARRIES A ROUTING DECISION MAKES IDEMPOTENCE PER-ROW, NOT PER-PASS. `assessment_id` includes the trigger, which is right — it is what says why analysis ran — but it means a re-run that routed differently does not address the row it is replacing, and an upsert cannot delete a row it is not addressing. The generalisation worth carrying: whenever an identifier includes something a re-run may legitimately decide differently, idempotence has to be enforced at the level of the thing that is being re-run (here, the pass over one context snapshot), not at the level of the key.

task 44: THE CLEANUP NEEDS NO READ PATH BECAUSE THE KEY SPACE IS ENUMERABLE. `helena.contracts.v1.AgentRequest` accepts exactly three (emitter, trigger) pairings, so the three identifiers one context version could ever hold are a pure function of the request. Addressing them by key rather than by a `SELECT` avoids the versioned reader task 45 still owes, avoids a FLUSH-ordering question inside the writer, and — the part that mattered — reaches ORPHANED CHILD ROWS, which a query keyed on what is present would never find because their parent row does not exist.

task 44: 'NO DURABLE IN-FLIGHT STATE OUTSIDE THE ENGINE' IS TESTABLE WITH A SIGKILLED CHILD PROCESS, AND CHEAPLY. The parent holds an endpoint that accepts the prompt and never answers, the child runs one assessment against it with HOME, TMPDIR and cwd pointed at three empty directories, and it is killed inside the first model call. Two details make it a proof rather than a gesture: assert the exit status IS -SIGKILL (an exception path would have run `finally` blocks and proved nothing), and set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE rather than allowing a .pyc exception — a test that allows one exception has to allow the next. `tests/test_orchestration.py::assess_at` is the module-level entry point the child imports.

task 44: COMPARING EVERY `helena.*` MODULE'S `__dict__` ACROSS A RUN NEEDS A WARM-UP RUN FIRST. Five modules (`contracts`, `policy`, `taxonomy`, `triage`, `rendering`, `hosts`) `import_module` their frozen version module on first use, which adds a name to the package's namespace. That is an import, not state, and without a preceding run the identity comparison fails on it. Run once, snapshot, run again, compare.

task 44: THE PACKAGE OPENS NO FILE FOR WRITING AT ALL, WHICH MAKES THE ASSERTION SIMPLE AND EXACT. `test_the_package_writes_no_file_anywhere` forbids `open`, the `Path` write/create methods, the `os` write calls and `tempfile`/`shutil` outright. Two false-positive traps found while writing it: `.replace(` and `.remove(` are string and list methods used all over the tree, so the `os` calls are matched only on an attribute whose value is the NAME `os`; and `helena.observability` calls `.write` on a stream ITS CALLER OPENED, which is why `write` is not on the list.

task 45: RISINGWAVE IGNORES THE LIBPQ `options=-csearch_path=...` STARTUP PARAMETER. Measured: a psycopg connection made with `?options=-csearch_path%3D<schema>` reports `current_schema()` as `public`, while `SET search_path TO <schema>` on the same connection works. So a SUBPROCESS cannot be pointed at the per-run schema `tests/conftest.py` builds, and any test of a command that reads the store has to either run in-process or grow a `--schema` flag that exists only for the test. This is why `tests/test_assessment_replay.py` tests the wrapper's argv in a subprocess and its printing in-process.

task 45: A CONTRACT MODEL WITH `strict=True` WILL NOT BUILD A NESTED MODEL FROM A DICT, BUT WILL FROM JSON. `Model.model_validate({...nested dict...})` fails in strict Python mode; `Model.model_validate_json(json.dumps(payload))` builds the whole tree. That is why the replay reader assembles a payload from the typed columns and hands it over as JSON — which is also the idiom `helena.contracts`' own docstring wrote down before anything used it. The one type the columns hold that JSON does not is `datetime`, handled by one `default=`.

task 45: THE STORED SCHEMA CANNOT REPRESENT AN EMPTY EVIDENCE PACKAGE. A package is written as its parts (patterns as rows, narrative as a column), so `EvidencePackage()` leaves no trace and comes back as no package — which the contract then refuses for an analyst verdict that is not `normal`. The reader raises `ReplayError` naming it rather than inventing an empty package. If a later increment wants that distinction it needs a column, not a reader change.

task 45: AN EMPTY ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE DOES NOT EXERCISE THE STARTUP-FAILURE PATH IN A SUBPROCESS. `Settings.load` treats empty as missing and then falls back to the `.env` file, as it is meant to — so `RISINGWAVE_DSN=''` in a subprocess env silently reads the developer's own DSN. Test that path through `helena.config` (which passes `env_file=None`), never through a subprocess.

task 45: `tests/test_assessments.py::an_assessment(analysis=...)` TAKES AN OUTCOME, NOT AN `analyst.Analysis` — it wraps one for you — and its default `triage_outcome` records `rendering_version='r1'`, a version no module implements. Anything that has to RE-RENDER (this task's whole point) must pass its own triage outcome and a version set whose `rendering_version` is `helena.rendering.v1.RENDERING_VERSION`, or the pairing check refuses the row at write time.

task 45: A REAL REPLAY AGAINST THE CONFIGURED MODEL ENDPOINT MOVES THE CONFIDENCE AND NOT THE PATH — one observation, on one context, so it is an anecdote and not a measurement. It is enough to say that the diff shape is the right shape: the thing that moved was the number `concept/04` calls 'a number to measure, not a routing constant'.

task 46: THE ENRICHED CONTEXT CANNOT BE THE SOURCE OF A STREAMING JOB, AND THAT DECIDES D7'S SHAPE. Measured 2026-09-11 on RisingWave 3.0.3: `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW probe AS SELECT context_id, status FROM helena_analytical_enriched_context` fails with `Bind error: failed to bind view helena_analytical_enriched_context`, because the view derives `status` from `now()` and `now()` outside a WHERE clause is rejected in a streaming query — the same thing sql/migrations/0009 measured for `completeness`. So there is no `CREATE SINK ... FROM helena_analytical_sink`; emission is Python reading a batch view and producing over the Kafka protocol. What DOES work in a batch view, checked at the same time: `array_agg(row(...))`, `jsonb_build_object`, `to_jsonb`, correlated self LEFT JOINs and `split_part`.

task 46: THE SINK TAKES ITS ENTITY LIST FROM `helena_signal_context_entities` AND NOT FROM THE ENRICHED CONTEXT, for the reason src/helena/rendering/__init__.py already gives: the enriched context CROSS JOINs the snapshot ledger, so on a deployment where no feed has ever loaded it yields NO ROWS AT ALL, and a message built on it would say a host contacted nothing when the only fault is that no loader has run. That turns into a FIFTH kind of absence in the emitted evidence — an entity whose evidence tuple is empty — which is not `missing` (a source that was asked for and had nothing to look in) and not `no_match` (a source that answered).

task 46: JOIN AN ASSESSMENT TO ITS CONTEXT ON `(context_id, context_version)` AND NOT ON THE ID ALONE. `context_version` is a digest over the context's own counters (0009), so a window that gained a late record has a different version under the same id, and joining on the id would put a later version's entities beside an earlier version's verdict. The sink carries `context_resolved` to say which happened, because an empty entity list that meant 'the store moved on' and an empty entity list that meant 'the host contacted nothing' would be the same bytes.

task 46: `helena_signal_host_context_live` IS BOUNDED BY THE RETENTION HORIZON (`window_end > now() - 24 hours`), SO THE COMMITTED CAPTURE'S OWN TIMESTAMPS ARE OUTSIDE IT. Any test that needs a live context has to re-stamp the records into the current window, which is what tests/test_rendering.py's `live` fixture does and what tests/test_sink.py now does. A test that ingests the capture as-is and then asks the live view for a context gets nothing and the failure reads as 'the capture produced no context'.

task 46: `tests/test_assessment_replay.py::test_the_column_list_is_the_one_the_engine_holds` QUERIES `information_schema.columns` WITHOUT A `table_schema = current_schema()` FILTER, so it fails if any OTHER schema on the same engine holds a `helena_analytical_assessment` — which is what a scratch schema left behind by an interactive session is. Two suite failures in this session (that one and tests/test_rendering.py::test_a_citation_resolves_to_evidence_the_rendering_actually_showed) were exactly this and nothing to do with the increment. Drop scratch schemas before running the suite, or add the filter.

task 46: PINNING A PYDANTIC MODEL'S `model_json_schema()` BYTE FOR BYTE PINS ITS DOCSTRINGS TOO — they arrive as `description` keys. A pin that turns every comment improvement into an 'interface change' teaches whoever hits it to regenerate the fixture reflexively, which is a pin that has stopped working. tests/test_sink.py::message_shape strips every `description` before comparing, so what is pinned is the field set, the types and which fields are required, which is what the interface actually is.

task 47: A `normal` TRIAGE RESULT CANNOT CARRY CITATIONS, and the contract enforces it: `AgentResult(classification='normal', citations=(...))` raises `a 'normal' triage decision returns verdict and confidence only (concept/04)`. That makes the `normal` message the one with the least in it, which is also why it is the one an emitter would be tempted to drop — so it is the first of the three outcomes in the emission test.

task 47: THE PINNED BROKER'S RECLAIM IS NOT INSTANT AND A TEST THAT ASSERTS AN EMPTY TOPIC IMMEDIATELY AFTER A DRAIN FAILS. Measured again here (it cost one red test): a second drain started right after the first still returned all three messages. tests/test_broker.py already measures this properly with a 45-second deadline and a control topic; anything else should assert on the ENGINE-side consequence rather than re-measure the broker.

task 47: AN `information_schema` QUERY IN A TEST MUST FILTER ON `table_schema = current_schema()`. Only one engine runs per machine, so a migrated dev store in `public` sits beside every test schema, and a query that builds an ordered LIST from an unfiltered result silently concatenates the two. This is the second session to hit it (task 46 recorded it; this one fixed the call site that fails). Running `scripts/migrate.py` against the dev store mid-session — which is what verifying an operator script requires — is enough to create the condition.

task 47: THE ENGINE-SIDE COUNT BELONGS IN A MIGRATION, NOT IN A PYTHON QUERY, and the reason is in what the count is for. The situation it answers is 'the consumer sees nothing and the broker has discarded everything', which is a situation where the operator is not running the emitter. A count that only exists as a method on `SinkStore` requires running Python to ask; `SELECT * FROM helena_analytical_emission_counts` does not. This is the same shape as `helena_ingest_counts` in 0004 and for the same reason.

task 47: READ THE LIST BEFORE THE COUNT, NOT AFTER. Both are reads of a store still being written to, and a pass landing between them has to fall on the side the counters can describe. List-then-count makes it raise `pending` — reported as 'run it again'. Count-then-list makes it raise `emitted` above `pending` and be refused as a double-emission that never happened.

task 47: `count(DISTINCT ...)` AND `GROUP BY` OVER THE SINK VIEW WORK IN A BATCH VIEW ON RISINGWAVE 3.0.3, which is not obvious given that the same view cannot be the source of a streaming job at all. The counter view is plain and is only ever read in batch; it could not be materialized even if that were wanted, for the reason 0019's head records.

task 48: A RATE BELONGS IN PYTHON AND ITS NUMERATOR AND DENOMINATOR BELONG IN SQL. A view cannot refuse a division, so a rate column would ship `0.0` as a fact in exactly the situation the number is being read to diagnose — nothing has run. Seven rates in this increment raise instead, and `helena.status.render` prints the refusal's own sentence where the number would have been rather than catching it and printing a zero. This is the same call task 12's `RetentionRejections.rate` and the normalizer's `QuarantineCounts.rate` already made.

task 48: `helena.status` CANNOT BE FOLDED INTO `helena.observability`, for a mechanical reason and not an aesthetic one: the metrics read `helena.enrichment`'s feed statuses so that `ok` / `stale` / `missing` are not respelled a fourth time, and `helena.enrichment` imports `helena.observability` for the redactor. One module is an import cycle. It is in `tests/test_package_layout.py`'s SUPPORT_MODULES rather than COMPONENT_MODULES because it is not a stage — it reads every stage's counters and owns none of them.

task 48: THE FIVE TERMS OF AN END-TO-END RECONCILIATION DO NOT FIT IN ONE VIEW IN A LAYERED SCHEMA, and the right answer is two views and an object that joins them, not a widened invariant. Widening `MAY_READ["analytical"]` to include `source` would license every future analytical view to skip the signal layer; a row-count view parked in the `flatten` layer would be formally legal and dishonest, since that layer is the flattening of nested observations and a count is not that.

task 48: WHAT RECONCILES AND WHAT MERELY REPORTS HAVE TO BE SEPARATED OR THE CHECK FIRES ON A HEALTHY PIPELINE. Refused: normalized + quarantined = admitted; admitted no greater than capture records; context records no greater than normalized; verdicts + typed failures = runs; cache hits + live queries = steps; escalations by trigger summing to escalations. Merely reported: `unaggregated` (a normalized event with no `ip` layer or an unparseable `ts` produces a flatten row the tumble drops — a fact about the input, and a pipeline that hid it could not tell anybody the input changed), and `emittable` against `assessments`, which differ legitimately whenever a pass escalated: two runs, one message.

task 48: AN ABSENT CAPTURE DIRECTORY IS SAID, NEVER DEFAULTED TO 0. How many records existed is a property of the retained file and of nothing else, because the broker is consume-once and restart-volatile, so `--captures` is optional and `0` would report a deployment that had lost every record it ever ingested. `PipelineReconciliation.unaccounted` raises when no capture directory was read.

task 48: A REPORT OVER A STORE STAMPS ONE MOMENT, AND IT HAS TO BE PASSED IN. `helena.status.report` takes `read_at` rather than calling `now()` itself: every staleness number in the result is relative to a moment, and a report that stamped itself would stamp a different moment than the `now()` the engine used inside the staleness view.

task 48: A MIGRATION THAT ADDS RELATIONS HAS TO EXTEND THE INVENTORY PINS IN OTHER TEST MODULES, and the full suite is the only thing that finds them -- this is the third increment in a row to learn it (task 46 recorded the class, task 47 hit one pin, this one hit two). The pins are deliberate friction and they are in modules the increment otherwise has no reason to open: tests/test_enriched.py holds the ORDERED list of analytical objects that read something (ordered, so it fails rather than merely being fragile), and tests/test_enrichment.py holds the reference layer's table/view inventory, as tests/test_context.py does for the signal layer. Adding a view in a layer means editing that layer's inventory in the same increment.

task 49: A conformance suite over a document has to read the document at run time, not copy it. `ROWS` holds each row verbatim and `_table()` re-parses `concept/07-principles.md` on every run, so a reworded row is red rather than silently leaving a test asserting a sentence nobody wrote any more. Copying the table into the test file once would have produced a gate that passes while checking the wrong thing.

task 49: Naming a row's in-depth coverage and RESOLVING the names is worth more than duplicating it. `COVERED_BY` maps each row to the `module::test` entries that hold it in depth, and a meta-test parses those files' ASTs to check every name still exists. That turns 'someone deleted the only test for this guarantee' into a failure at the row, and it cost about sixty lines instead of a second copy of the fifteen-case composition table.

task 49: Read source with `ast`, not with `re`, when the question is 'does this module do X'. Three checks in this module were written as text searches first and all three were wrong in the same way: `src/helena/agents.py` quotes `concept/07`'s 'Secrets and configuration' heading, so `\bSecret\b` matched prose; `src/helena/context.py`'s own docstring says 'retention is a filter, not a delete', so a search for DELETE found the sentence arguing for the thing's absence. `_names()` (identifiers referenced as code) and `_statements()` (string literals that are not docstrings) are the two helpers that fixed it, and they are the same lesson `prds/CONTEXT.md` already records about asserting on SQL text.

task 49: Hard-wrapped Markdown defeats substring matching. The sentences MNH-19 and MNH-20 require to be present span a newline in README.md, so `sentence in path.read_text()` failed on the wrapping rather than on the claim. `_prose()` collapses whitespace before matching.

task 49: A disclaimer contains the claim it disclaims. MNH-20's first version flagged `docs/overview-slides.md`'s own 'Nothing here claims the verdicts are right.' A forbidden-claim regex over prose needs a negation guard on the text preceding the match, or it fails on exactly the sentence it exists to require.

task 49: The three failure modes of a gate are worth inducing before trusting it. Appending a row to the note, renaming a conformance test, and breaking a `COVERED_BY` reference were each done to the working tree, run, observed red, and reverted. Two of them would have passed silently under the first implementation: `test_every_row_of_the_table_has_a_test_named_for_it` originally iterated `ROWS` rather than the note, so a row added to `concept/` was caught only after someone had already copied it into the test file.

task 50: A dependency boundary is not a store boundary, and the difference is the standard library. `tests/test_dependency_boundary.py` allows every name in `sys.stdlib_module_names` — it has to, the package is mostly standard library — so `import sqlite3`, `import shelve` and `import dbm` passed it by construction. The single-store invariant in concept/instruction.md §2 forbids 'no second database, no vector store, no checkpoint store, no file-backed agent memory', and not one of those four requires an install. Any future 'we have a test for that' about a store should be checked against whether the store needs a dependency at all.

task 50: The persistence target that no import scan can see is the one defined in SQL. `CREATE SINK ... WITH (connector = 'kafka', ...)` is a second egress channel with its own credentials, `CREATE SOURCE` with an S3 or Iceberg connector is a second store, and `CREATE SECRET` is a credential outside the environment. RisingWave exposes all four in `rw_catalog.rw_sources` / `rw_sinks` / `rw_connections` / `rw_secrets`, each carrying `schema_id`, so the query scopes cleanly to the migrated schema via `rw_catalog.rw_schemas`. Note that `rw_schemas` has columns (id, name, owner, acl) only — `current_schema()` cannot be joined in a subquery against it the way information_schema allows, so resolve the id in Python and parameterize.

task 50: Scope a source scan by what the name can also mean, or it gets widened until it checks nothing. The filesystem-write scan names six methods — write_text, write_bytes, touch, mkdir, makedirs, symlink_to — and deliberately not `write`, `remove`, `rename` or `replace`: helena.observability writes a log line to a TextIO and `str.replace` / `dataclasses.replace` are used throughout, so a scan for those fires on code that is not about files. `open()` is judged by its mode instead of its presence, with an unreadable mode treated as a write. This is task 49's ast-not-regex lesson one level down: the false positive is not prose here, it is a method name with a second meaning.

task 50: `uv run` installs what `pyproject.toml` declares, whether or not you asked it to. Editing the dependency list to induce a test failure put langgraph, langchain-core, langgraph-checkpoint, redis and about twenty transitive packages into `.venv/` — the very SDKs three tests exist to keep out. `uv.lock` was NOT modified (git status confirmed) and `uv sync` restored the environment exactly, but the window between the two is a suite that could have gone green or red for the wrong reason. Revert the file and run `uv sync` in the same command as the mutation, and check `ls .venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages` rather than trusting the revert.

task 50: A meta-test over a concept note must fail in both directions or it only enforces half the rule. `test_the_technology_table_still_records_each_rejection` catches a row reworded or reversed; `test_every_rejection_in_the_technology_table_has_a_test_here` catches a row added with nothing carrying it. Neither forbids the note from changing — concept/ is the authority — what they forbid is the note changing without the decision record and the test landing in the same commit.

deferred: "Route EVERY outbound-request log and every exception carrying a request URL through the redactor" — the mechanism is built and is the only way to log a request, but there is no outbound request anywhere in the package yet (no HTTP client, no loader, no model call), so there are zero call sites to route. The increment that adds the first fetch owns using `outbound_request` and `exception` rather than `info` with a raw URL.

Routing third-party stdlib `logging` records (psycopg, confluent-kafka) into this channel, or silencing them. No handler is configured, so their records currently go nowhere. Belongs to the increment that first runs one of those clients against a real service.
A log level below `info` and any level filtering or sampling. LEVELS is (info, warning, error); a level nothing emits is a config key with one value.

Binding event_id/context_id onto a logger once instead of passing them per call. Every call site is explicit for now; a `.bound()` helper is worth adding when a stage actually logs in a loop over one context.

Any counter or metric surface. `concept/07-principles.md` requires latency, cost, staleness, error, escalation and record counts to be observable, but those are typed columns on stored rows — the store, not the log — and the tables do not exist yet.
02.makes_buildable: Every later increment has a log channel it does not have to design: `logger(component, settings)` gives a StructuredLogger carrying tenant and sensor, and `log.outbound_request(...)` / `log.exception(...)` are the two calls a feed loader or an MCP provider tool makes around a fetch. `Redactor.url` is the helper the loader uses on the URL it records as provenance, so the provenance row and the log line are redacted by the same code. The D1 normalizer has `event_id` and the D2 context builder has `context_id` as first-class record fields, and anything citing versions has `versions`. The hosted-tracing boundary test means the LangChain/model-client increment cannot pull a tracer in transitively without failing the suite.
02.next_session_should_know: Log through `helena.observability.logger(component, settings)` and nothing else — `print()` and stdlib `logging` inside `helena` are a test failure (tests/test_observability.py::test_the_package_has_no_second_logging_path), and so is importing or installing any hosted tracing SDK (tests/test_dependency_boundary.py, two tests). The record has ten fixed top-level keys; your own fields are keyword arguments and land nested under `fields`, so you cannot shadow `tenant`. `event` is the dotted name of what happened; `event_id` is the normalizer's flow-event identity and `context_id` the host-context identity, both keyword arguments, both null when absent. `versions={}` raises — pass the real version set or omit it. A field that will not JSON-serialize raises TypeError rather than being repr'd, so convert datetimes at the call site. For anything with a URL: `log.outbound_request(event, method=..., url=...)` and `log.exception(event, exc, ...)` — never `log.info(..., url=raw_url)`, even though the emitter would catch a configured credential anyway. `Redactor.url(...)` is also the helper for the provenance URL a loader stores, so the row and the log line get identical treatment; build one with `Redactor.from_settings(settings)`. deferred: The requiredness of every field is derived from one capture — 62 records, one host, 130.8 s — because that is the only flow-record corpus that exists. `data/ingest/README.md` warns explicitly that this capture's ratios describe the capture and not the schema, so a field required here because 15 observations all carried it may be optional in reality, and a producer omitting it will be QUARANTINED rather than accepted. That is the intended direction of the error (drift surfaces, countable, raw record kept), but the quarantine rate is the number to watch when a second capture arrives, and the answer to a high one is a new observation of the input, not a field loosened on a hunch. Rule applied and recorded in docs/decisions/0010: present only if observed; required if present in every observation of its kind; optional if the sample shows it absent at least once, including when the counter-example comes from the other HTTP version.

Cross-field validation that `ip.proto` agrees with which of `tcp`/`udp` is present. True on all 62 records and asserted nowhere, because it is a property of this producer rather than a rule of the input — enforcing it would quarantine the first ICMP record ever sent.

Parsing is normalization and belongs to the increments that do it; the host-part rule applies where a domain column is written, not where the record is read.

The adapter protocol, the typed parse-failure envelope and quarantine — tasks 8 and 9. A record that fails validation raises a `ValidationError` and nothing catches it yet; inventing a failure type here would be a contract written ahead of the code that stores it.

Identity stamping, the event id and the schema version — task 7. The schema version is stamped on the normalized event, not on the raw record: the raw record is what arrived and the producer sends no version.

Logging. `helena.observability.logger` needs `Settings` for tenant and sensor, and reading a file to count its records does not need an identity. The increment that consumes the ingest topic already has one.

Task 8 (adapter protocol) has the one format's model to write the first adapter around, and `read_capture` handing over undecoded bytes is the shape a parse failure has to keep. Task 9 (quarantine) has the typed failures to route — `ValidationError` from the contract, `CaptureError` from the registry — and a contract that refuses drift rather than coercing it, so there is something to quarantine. Tasks 10 and 11 have `record_count` and `byte_size` as the reconciliation denominator that the consume-once broker cannot supply, and `scan_captures` as the hash-to-file lookup `helena replay-capture <hash>` needs. Task 12 onward has fixture captures that exercise every layer combination, a null application layer and an empty-but-observed array, so a flatten view can be tested on the case that distinguishes 'no DNS traffic' from 'DNS traffic with no answers'.

Read a capture through `describe_capture(path)` / `read_capture(capture)` / `scan_captures(directory)` and parse a record with `FlowRecord.model_validate_json(line)` — do not write a second reader, because replay must exercise the same path as live ingestion and a parallel one is what `concept/03-architecture.md` forbids. `read_capture` yields `(offset, raw bytes)` with `offset` the zero-based ordinal in the file and the line undecoded, which is what a quarantine row needs; it re-hashes the file and raises `CaptureError` if the content changed since the `Capture` was described, so do not hold a description across a write. Four things that will bite otherwise. (1) The contract is `strict=True` + `extra="forbid"` + `frozen=True`: any drift — an unknown key, a number sent as a string, a missing field — is a `ValidationError`, and NOTHING catches it yet. Task 8's adapter and task 9's quarantine are what turn it into a typed row; until then a bad record kills the caller. (2) The requiredness of every field comes from one 62-record capture and is the likeliest source of a false quarantine on real traffic — docs/decisions/0010-capture-identity.md has the rule and what to do about a high quarantine rate, and the answer is a new observation of the input, not a loosened field. (3) `as_supplied()` is `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)`, and the 62-record round-trip test is what enforces 'no invented fields' — adding a field to any model in the contract will fail 62 tests at once, which is deliberate: a field on the input contract that no producer sends is where a defaulted tenant comes from. (4) Capture identity is the sha256 of the FILE, so the same record in two files belongs to two captures with different references — which is why a raw-record reference is the capture plus an offset and never the record's own `id` (that is the producer's label, `udp.0`/`tcp.17`, unique only within a capture and scoped by protocol). The fixtures are `tests/fixtures/captures/<sha256>.jsonl` with a README mapping each digest to what it holds; every record in them is a byte-for-byte copy of a line of `data/ingest/flow-sample.jsonl`, and nothing in them is synthesised on purpose. If a stored event ever needs to say it, that is a contract change and a decision.

One adapter per deployment is deliberate: sniffing would make 'which parser produced this row' a property of the row rather than of the configuration, and a record that parsed as two formats would be resolved by whichever adapter was tried first. Six things that will bite otherwise. (1) `normalize` NO LONGER RAISES on a bad record: it returns `NormalizedEvent | ParseFailure`, and so does every element `normalize_capture` yields. Code that assumes an event will happily read `.identity` off a failure — `isinstance(result, ParseFailure)` is the check, and `enumerate` over `normalize_capture` gives each result its offset because there is exactly one result per record in file order. `normalize` still RAISES `CaptureError` for an offset that addresses no record; that is this deployment's bug, not input drift, and quarantining it would file a producer's name against our own mistake. (2) `HELENA_INPUT_FORMAT` is a new required variable. It is in the local `.env` as `flow-json`, in `.env.example` and in `helena.config.REQUIRED_VARIABLES`; an environment without it fails at startup naming it. `helena.config` does not validate the value — `helena.normalizer.adapter_for` does, raising `ConfigurationError` naming the variable and listing the registered formats. (3) The three parse-failure reasons must stay distinct all the way into task 9's table and counter: `malformed_json` (framing broke), `not_this_format` (wrong adapter configured), `contract_violation` (producer drift — the rate ADR-0010 says to watch). They are not equally precise: `flow-json` cannot report `not_this_format` for another format's JSON object because it has no envelope to check, and a test pins that asymmetry. (4) Adding a third input format is an adapter class, an entry in `INPUT_ADAPTERS` and a configuration value — never a contract change, and a test asserts the event contract has no field naming a format. If a format ever needs one, that is an escalation. (5) `tests/fixtures/captures/` is `flow-json` only; the second format's fixture is in `tests/fixtures/captures-flow-envelope/` and dropping a non-`flow-json` file into the first directory fails a dozen contract tests, because `FIXTURE_LINES` sweeps it. `flow-envelope` is synthetic — nothing sends it, it exists so the boundary claim is measured — and it should keep that label wherever it is mentioned. (6) Still true from task 7 and unchanged: no engine table holds an event, `EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` still has one home and needs its SQL copy plus equality test in the increment that first stores an event, capture identity is provisional under live ingestion (ADR-0010), and there is still no git repository, so nothing here was committed. `bin/README.md` still points at a `scripts/build-binaries.sh` that does not exist.
08.summary: `helena.normalizer` now reads its input through an adapter selected by `HELENA_INPUT_FORMAT`: `parse(line: bytes) -> FlowRecord | ParseFailure`, with no capture, no identity and no configuration, so an adapter cannot stamp a tenant, decide an event id or add a field to the event. Two are registered — `flow-json`, the format every real capture is in, and `flow-envelope`, a deliberately trivial synthetic second format — and a refused record now comes back as a typed `ParseFailure` (`malformed_json` / `not_this_format` / `contract_violation`) rather than as an exception, so a bad record does not stall the capture. 89 new tests; the suite is 396 passed.

deferred: The 'ingest counters' half of PRD step 3. The step says 'expose a quarantine rate counter ALONGSIDE the ingest counters' and there are no ingest counters — task 10's own steps are where 'records consumed, normalized, quarantined' is listed, and nothing consumes from a broker or stores a normalized event yet. What exists is the quarantine counter with the only denominator that exists (`Capture.record_count`, because the broker is consume-once), so the rate is computable and reconciles today; `QuarantineCounts.normalized` is a documented subtraction, exact because `normalize_capture` yields exactly one result per record, and it is the value task 10's engine-side count should reconcile against.

A timestamp column on a quarantine row. Deliberate and argued in ADR-0013: a wall clock makes a replayed capture produce a different row from the run it replays (ADR-0011's reason for keeping one off the event), and under the upsert the stored value would silently mean 'the last time this was refused'. When a record arrived is a property of an ingest run, and nothing records runs yet — the increment that does owns adding it.

A version set on the quarantine row. `VersionSet` requires all eight dimensions and seven do not exist yet (ADR-0008); stamping one here means inventing seven constants for a row no assessment cites. The two things that actually determined the row are recorded: `schema_version` (EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION, the contract that refused it) and `input_format`. ADR-0012 deferred 'an adapter version on ParseFailure' to this increment — adapters still have no version of their own, and this table is where one belongs when they do.

Routing `CaptureError` to quarantine. An offset that addresses no record still raises, unchanged from task 8: the bytes were never read, so it is this deployment's bug rather than input drift, and quarantining it would file a producer's name against our own mistake. So 'route EVERY typed parse or validation failure' is scoped to the ones that are facts about the input — the three ParseFailure reasons.

Logging. Nothing on this path emits a log line, for the same reason tasks 7 and 8 gave: `helena.observability.logger` needs Settings and there is no ingest run to attribute a line to. The counter is a store query, which is the more durable surface anyway.

A second copy of EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION in SQL. Task 7's handover said the increment that first creates a table holding a normalized event must add the SQL copy and the equality test. This table holds records that did NOT become events, and the version is written as data by the one Python constant rather than declared as a literal in the migration — so there is still no second copy to drift, and the obligation still belongs to the increment that stores an event.

Truncation of a large payload. Nothing truncates, so there is no visible-truncation marker to design. If a producer ever sends a line large enough to matter, adding a limit means adding the marker with it — `concept/instruction.md` §2, truncation is visible or it is a bug.
09.makes_buildable: Task 10 (broker wiring) has the destination for the refusals it will consume and the one call that routes them — `Normalizer.ingest_capture` — so the consumer does not need its own quarantining path, and it has two of its three ingest counters already reconciling (`QuarantineCounts.records/quarantined/by_reason`); the third, `normalized`, is a subtraction here and becomes an engine-side count in the increment that stores an event, reconciling against this subtraction rather than replacing it. Task 11 (replay driver) has the idempotence it needs: re-ingesting a capture rewrites the same quarantine rows rather than doubling them, so a replayed capture does not inflate the rate — tested. Task 12 (flatten layer) has the pattern for a migration that creates a table and a plain view over it and asserts the Python name constants against information_schema by asking the engine. Anything watching for input drift has the number ADR-0010 said to watch, with a runbook section (docs/runbook.md §6) saying what each reason means and that the answer to a high rate is a new observation of the input, not a loosened field.

Build the quarantine with `Quarantine(connection=<psycopg autocommit connection>, identity=settings.identity)`. Six things that will bite otherwise. (1) `ingest_capture` REFUSES a quarantine whose identity is not the normalizer's, with a `ConfigurationError` — the two are configured from the same `Settings` and that is the only combination that works, deliberately. (2) The quarantine primary key is (tenant, sensor, capture_sha256, record_offset); re-ingesting rewrites the same rows rather than doubling, so replay does not inflate the rate — do not add a timestamp or an event id to the row without reading ADR-0013 first, both were rejected on purpose. (3) `QuarantineCounts` refuses to exist if its numbers do not reconcile, and `by_reason` always carries all three reasons including zeros; `normalized` is `records - quarantined`, a subtraction that is exact only because `normalize_capture` yields one result per record — task 10's engine-side normalized count should reconcile AGAINST it, not replace it. (4) A rate over a capture with no records raises rather than returning 0.0. (5) Writes do not FLUSH; the two read methods do, so a count taken from a different connection mid-run may lag. (6) `CaptureError` (an offset addressing no record) still raises and is NOT quarantined — that is this deployment's bug, not the producer's. docs/runbook.md §6 is the operator's page for all of it, including what a rising `contract_violation` rate means and that the answer is a new observation of the input rather than a loosened field. Note the runbook's old '§6 When something is wrong' is now §7; nothing referenced it by number. Still true and unchanged: no event is stored in the engine, nothing consumes from the broker, `EVENT_SCHEMA_VERSION` still has one home (this table writes it as data, not as a SQL literal, so there is still no second copy to assert equal), capture identity is provisional under live ingestion (ADR-0010), `bin/README.md` still points at a `scripts/build-binaries.sh` that does not exist, and there is still no git repository, so nothing here was committed. One small stale statement noticed and left alone: `docs/decisions/0007-sql-migrations.md` says `sql/migrations/` holds the ledger and nothing else — true when it was written at D0, false since migration 0002, and it is a dated record rather than a live claim.
09.summary: Quarantine now lives in the engine. `sql/migrations/0003_ingest_quarantine.sql` creates `helena_ingest_quarantine` — ingestion identity, raw-record reference, the contract version that refused it, the typed ParseFailure and the payload as BYTEA exactly as read, keyed on (tenant, sensor, capture_sha256, record_offset) — plus the plain view `helena_ingest_quarantine_counts` grouped by reason. `helena.normalizer.Quarantine` writes and reads them and `Normalizer.ingest_capture(capture, quarantine)` is the ingestion path: it yields the events, routes every refusal to the table with its raw line, and carries on. `QuarantineCounts` joins the engine-side numerator to the capture's own record count and refuses a total that does not reconcile. 13 new tests, the engine-side ones executed against a real RisingWave; the suite is 409 passed.

deferred: `helena replay-capture <hash>` and the publishing helper it will own — that is task 11. The test suite publishes a capture in three lines using IngestMessage and BrokerProducer; a helper in the package with only a test calling it would be structure ahead of the increment.
The output topic: no HELENA_OUTPUT_TOPIC, no egress producer call site. See invariant_conflicts.
A long-running consumer. `BrokerConsumer.consume` is bounded by an idle timeout because a bounded ingest run is what exists to be reconciled; a daemon that never returns has no caller yet.

Consuming across more than one partition. The pinned broker runs one partition per topic and fanning out would be ordering machinery for a case that does not exist; the partition is a parameter with one value in use.
Any use of blink's REST port (30004). Deliberately unreachable, and tests/test_broker.py asserts helena/broker.py imports no HTTP or socket module.

The whole of it is exercised end to end in tests/test_normalizer.py against the real broker and engine; copy `publish()` and `consumed_messages()` from that file into the replay driver rather than reinventing the framing. Eight things that will bite otherwise. (1) HELENA_INGEST_TOPIC is a NEW required variable — it is in helena.config.VARIABLES, .env.example and the local .env, and any test that builds an environment dict must include it or Settings.load fails naming it. (2) `settings.infrastructure.ingest_topic` is where it lands; there is no output topic and adding one is task 46's. (3) `helena.broker` is the ONLY module allowed to import confluent_kafka — tests/test_broker.py fails on a second importer, on an unapproved name bound from it, on an HTTP or socket import inside broker.py, and on ANY address-shaped string literal anywhere in src/helena (including a `:9092`-style port). Put an address in configuration, and put a measured fact about the broker in a docstring (docstrings are excluded from that scan on purpose). (4) `create_topic` asks Metadata first — do not rewrite it as create-and-catch, blink answers a duplicate create with an unparseable response. (5) `publish` is asynchronous; nothing has reached the broker until `flush()`, which RAISES on outstanding or refused messages. The `with BrokerProducer(...)` block flushes on clean exit. (6) The reclaim after a drain is asynchronous — do not write a test asserting a topic is empty immediately, and do not build a retry that re-reads a topic. Replay publishes the retained capture. (8) `IngestCounts` refuses a set that does not reconcile and `complete is False` means records were lost between the producer and the store — the capture is still on disk, replay it. Docs: docs/decisions/0014-the-ingest-topic-message.md is the wire contract and the broker-is-not-a-store measurements; docs/runbook.md gained §7 (ingest and the four counters) and its §3 now carries the corrected CreateTopics and reclaim measurements; the old §7 troubleshooting table is now §8 and has four new rows.

deferred: A `helena` console entry point, and a Makefile target. `make migrate` takes no arguments; a replay target would need CAPTURES and a hash, which is a configuration surface for one command.

A long-running consumer. `--ingest` drains the topic once and stops on the idle timeout, which is what a bounded, reconcilable run is; a daemon is still task 10's deferred item and still has no caller.

Replaying a directory, a range of captures, or a time window. One capture per invocation; a loop in a shell covers the rest, and 'which captures cover this window' needs a capture index, which would be the second store §2 forbids.
Rate as anything but a floor. A pacer that caught up after a slow broker by publishing a burst would replay at a rate nobody asked for; the docstring and the runbook state the choice.
Counting messages on the topic that belong to another capture. `IngestCounts` refuses the set instead, loudly and by name. Splitting the count would be machinery for a producer that does not exist.
11.makes_buildable: Task 12 (flatten-layer views) can populate a throwaway store from a capture in one call and, more usefully, does not have to be written before the data exists — a flatten view added over `helena_normalized_events` backfills, measured. Any later view layer (signal, analytical) inherits that. `publish_capture` is also the only producer this project has for the ingest topic, so anything that needs records on the topic — a live-consumer daemon, a load or latency measurement, an evaluation run — uses it rather than open-coding the headers. `consume_ingest_topic` is the consumer half a daemon would call, already the only place a wire message becomes an ingest message.
11.next_session_should_know: Replay is `uv run scripts/replay_capture.py --captures <dir> <sha256> [--rate N] [--ingest] [--idle-timeout S]`, and `tests/fixtures/captures/` is a capture directory (files are named by their own digest; `data/ingest/` is NOT one — flow-sample.jsonl fails the name check, which is deliberate). Underneath it are two new functions in `helena.normalizer`: `publish_capture(capture, producer, topic, rate=None)` creates the topic, publishes every record with the reference in its headers, flushes, and returns the count; `consume_ingest_topic(consumer, topic, idle_timeout=...)` is a generator turning wire messages into `IngestMessage`s and is the one place that decode happens. A live consumer daemon should call exactly those two, not reimplement the framing. Five things worth knowing before touching this. (1) A view added over `helena_normalized_events` BACKFILLS — measured, and it contradicts `concept/06-technology.md`; docs/runbook.md §5 and the new §8 carry the measurement, and the concept note itself has not been edited (concept/ outranks code, so that correction is the operator's). Task 12's flatten views therefore do not need to exist before data flows; what needs to exist before data flows is the events table. (2) `IngestCounts._reconciles` changed order: `consumed > records` is now checked first and says 'consumed more than once', because the upsert makes a double-consumed run arithmetically identical to a lossy one. No field changed and no caller changed. (3) `--ingest` makes the replay process the consumer too. That is right only while nothing else consumes the topic — which is the case today. (4) `--rate` is a floor, not a schedule, and a rate of zero or less is refused rather than read as 'unpaced'. (5) The runbook grew §8 (replay, the capture-directory rule, the two-replays-vs-two-publishes distinction, and the backfill procedure) and the old §8 troubleshooting table is now §9 with four new rows; README gained a 'Replay' subsection under ingest. Nothing else in the tree moved.

The two halves of the wire — `publish_capture` and `consume_ingest_topic` — live in `helena.normalizer` beside the code live traffic already uses, so there is one adapter, one `_stamp` and one pair of stores rather than a replay pipeline beside the real one.

A scheduler. 'On its own schedule' is scripts/load_public_suffix_list.py run by cron, a timer or a hand. Nothing in this repository schedules anything and a scheduler with its own state would be a second store (concept/instruction.md §2).

15.next_session_should_know: Migration 0008 adds seven objects. Two tables with a writer -- `helena_reference_public_suffix` (snapshot_version, rule, suffix, is_wildcard, is_exception, section; PK (rule, suffix)) and `helena_reference_public_suffix_load` (attempted_at, source_url, status, snapshot_version, rule_count, failure_reason, failure_detail; PK (attempted_at, source_url)) -- plus `helena_reference_public_suffix_load_counts`, a plain view mirroring helena_ingest_quarantine_counts. A consumer that collapses any two of them into a NULL breaks concept/instruction.md §2. (3) The table holds exactly one snapshot at a time and the derivation GROUPs BY snapshot_version rather than taking max(), so a two-snapshot table produces two rows per name and fails the one-row-per-name assertion loudly instead of being silently decided by whichever digest sorts higher. The redactor parameter is required rather than optional, deliberately. (6) The source URL lives in scripts/load_public_suffix_list.py and nowhere else -- the package may not hold one, and test_no_module_in_the_package_holds_a_broker_address is what enforces that. The next feed's URL belongs in its own script for the same reason. (7) The suite now makes two live HTTP requests to publicsuffix.org and skips them when the machine has no route. Four things to know before adding an object. (1) YOUR CREATE NEEDS A DECLARATION BLOCK immediately above it, no blank line, with Layer / Object / Reads / Read by. `Reads:` must be a comma-separated list of relation names or the word `nothing` (a note may follow the first sentence); `Read by:` is prose, and a relation is recognised in it by the helena_ prefix. (2) YOU MUST ALSO EDIT THE FILES YOU READ FROM: every relation you declare in `Reads:` has to name you in its own `Read by:`, or test_every_relation_that_reads_an_object_is_named_in_its_read_by fails. (3) The layers are operational / source / reference / flatten / signal / analytical, and the first analytical object may read signal and reference only. Adding a layer means adding a row to MAY_READ, which a test asserts. Before emitting any path: it must be in the version's vocabulary, its root must equal its first segment, and the root must be open to your level and your emitter. The evidence level is five roots and no children, and that is not an omission to be helpfully filled in -- see the assumption above before adding one. Anomaly, baseline and novelty paths are declared and marked unused with a shared reason: every one is a comparison against this host's past, and a context is one host in one five-minute window.
